LIKE MANY Humble Dollar readers, you may be the super saver of the family. So, here’s a public service announcement: The maximum IRA contribution will remain $7,500 in 2027, unless you’re 50 or older, in which case you can add $1,100 in catch-up contributions.
p

You may pass this news along to your offspring—possibly along with a Christmas check to encourage their savings habits. Not everyone is eligible, of course. You need earned income but not too much. In 2027, Roth IRA eligibility starts phasing out at $250,000 for married couples and $158,000 for single filers—a high enough limbo bar for most kids to pass under, I imagine.
p

There’s more to be saved in the 401(k) next year, but this may be an action item for you or a pal who is still grinding away. The IRS announced on November 12 that the basic maximum contribution to 401(k) and 403(b) plans will be $25,500 in 2027. That’s $1,000 more than 2026 thanks to the inflation escalator built into the law.
p

Workers aged 50 and older in 2027 can add catch-up contributions, but this gets a little complicated. Let’s start with the base case: If you’ll be age 50 to 59 or 64 and older any time in 2027, you can save an additional $8,500 in catch-up contributions. That’s $500 more than this year.
p

Workers who will be 60, 61, 62, or 63 in 2027, however, can make ‘super-catch-up’ contributions of $11,750 instead of $8,500. Here’s the complication. If the worker earns more than $150,000 in 2026, the super catch-up must be made in after-tax Roth contributions, if the plan allows.
p

To ring that top bell, it pays to start early. Some plans, like IBM’s, offer a ‘max out’ button on their website so workers don’t have to lift a finger to capture more savings in the New Year. Otherwise, you (or your child or your pal) will need to raise your savings rate, which is expressed as a percentage of annual pay.
p
To use an easy example, a worker making $100,000 a year would have to save 26% of pay all year to reach the contribution maximum of $25,500 in 2027.
p
Someone age 60 who is making $100,000 would need to contribute 38% to save the maximum of $37,250, which is the base rate plus the super catch-up.
p
With numbers that steep—and the daunting cost of living—it’s easy to see why just one in seven (14%) workers saved the maximum in 2025, according to plan provider Vanguard Group.
p
Being a supersaver is a challenge, no question. As you may have observed, however, it’s a great behavior to model for your family. Saving is catching, no question.
